opus-5.5.text:
I think the DoNotPay case is a really instructive example, precisely because it's so unglamorous. DoNotPay marketed itself as "the world's first robot lawyer." They claimed their AI could replace human lawyers, draft legally sound documents, even help you sue people. And the FTC basically said: you never tested whether this actually worked, you didn't have attorneys checking the outputs, and you can't make those claims without evidence. That's it. They didn't need a new AI statute to do that. It's just good old-fashioned consumer protection law against deceptive advertising.

What I find important about it is that it cuts against a narrative that's very common in AI policy debates, which is that AI is this fundamentally new thing, our laws are hopelessly outdated, and nothing can be done until Congress passes some sweeping AI act. A lot of the harms people actually experience from AI aren't exotic. They're companies overpromising what a product can do, selling snake oil essentially. And regulators already have the authority to go after that. The FTC has been quite explicit about this, saying there's no AI exemption from the laws on the books.

Now, I don't want to overstate it. The penalty was fairly modest, and enforcement is always after the fact. Someone has to get harmed, or at least misled, first. And there are genuine gaps where existing law doesn't map neatly onto what AI systems do. But I'd argue we should start by asking what existing agencies can already do, and invest in their capacity, technical expertise, staffing, before assuming we need brand new frameworks. Often the bottleneck isn't the absence of law; it's the absence of enforcement resources.

And there's a broader lesson for the industry too. A lot of the hype around AI products lives in that gap between what's claimed and what's been validated. Cases like this send a signal that if you're going to say your product does something, you'd better have evidence. That's a pretty healthy norm to reinforce.

r001.rationale: The response says the FTC used existing consumer protection law against deceptive advertising and did not need a new AI statute.

r002.rationale: It urges starting with what existing agencies can do and investing in their capacity before assuming new frameworks are needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the DoNotPay case is actually one of my favorite examples, because it cuts against this narrative that we constantly hear, which is that AI is moving so fast that the law can't possibly keep up, and so we need some brand new regulatory apparatus designed specifically for AI. And what the DoNotPay case shows is that a lot of the harms we're worried about are actually pretty old harms, and we already have tools for dealing with them.

So just to recap for listeners: DoNotPay marketed itself as "the world's first robot lawyer." The claim was that you could use this AI to sue people, to fight parking tickets, to generate legal documents, essentially to replace a human lawyer. And the FTC's complaint was, in a sense, very boring. They didn't say anything about AI being dangerous or about model capabilities or alignment. They said: you made claims about what your product could do, you didn't test whether the product could actually do those things, and consumers were harmed as a result. That's deceptive advertising. That's Section 5 of the FTC Act, which is from 1914.

And I think that's exactly the right frame. One of the things Sayash Kapoor and I argue in the book is that a lot of what gets called "AI harm" is really just the harm of selling something that doesn't work, and dressing it up with the word AI to make it sound more credible than it is. The FTC had this whole initiative they called "Operation AI Comply," and DoNotPay was one of several cases, and the throughline across all of them was that the AI label was being used as a kind of marketing magic to escape scrutiny.

Now, I don't want to overstate it. The settlement was something like $193,000, which is not going to strike fear into the heart of any well-funded company. And the FTC is resource constrained; they can't go after every snake-oil AI product out there. So I'm not saying existing law is sufficient for everything. There are genuine gaps, especially around things like transparency about training data, or about how these systems get deployed in high-stakes settings like hiring or criminal justice.

But what I'd push back on is the instinct to start from scratch. If you look at the actual harms people are experiencing from AI today, a lot of them fall squarely within the jurisdiction of existing regulators: the FTC for consumer protection, the EEOC for discrimination in hiring, the CFPB for credit decisions, state attorneys general for fraud. These agencies already have the authority. What they often lack is the technical capacity and the political will, and sometimes the budget. So to me the policy question is less "what new AI law do we need" and more "how do we empower the regulators we already have to actually enforce the laws we already have." The DoNotPay case is a small but, I think, pretty clear proof of concept that this can work.

r001.rationale: The response says the FTC addressed untested claims about DoNotPay’s capabilities as deceptive advertising under Section 5 of the FTC Act, a law dating to 1914.

r002.rationale: It argues against starting from scratch and urges empowering existing regulators to enforce existing laws, rather than waiting for new AI legislation.

astra-6.text:
I think it illustrates that we’re not starting from scratch when it comes to regulating AI. We already have laws against deceptive marketing, and those laws apply whether a product uses AI or not. If you market something as an AI lawyer, you need evidence to support the claims you’re making about what it can do. Calling it AI doesn’t exempt you from that obligation.

So the FTC’s action against DoNotPay is an example of using existing consumer protection authority to hold a company accountable for its claims. That won’t address every risk from AI, and there are legitimate questions about where we need new laws. But enforcing the laws we already have is a substantial part of the answer, especially when it comes to exaggerated claims about AI capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says the FTC used existing consumer protection authority and explains that deceptive marketing laws apply to AI products and their claims.

r002.rationale: It advocates enforcing laws already in place as a substantial part of regulating AI, while recognizing that new laws may also be needed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a good example of how we don’t need to start from scratch with AI regulation. The FTC’s authority to go after deceptive business practices applies whether a company is selling an AI product or anything else. If you claim that your AI can do the work of a lawyer, you need evidence to back that up. Calling it AI doesn’t exempt you from that obligation.

That’s especially important because consumers often can’t evaluate these claims themselves. Someone looking for affordable legal help may have no way of knowing whether the advice they’re getting is reliable. So putting the burden on the company to substantiate its claims is a very useful intervention.

It doesn’t mean existing laws solve every problem with AI. But there’s a lot we can accomplish by enforcing the laws we already have, instead of treating every AI-related harm as something entirely new that requires an entirely new legal framework.

r001.rationale: The response says the FTC can use its authority over deceptive business practices to challenge unsupported AI claims, which conveys reliance on existing authority to police deceptive marketplace claims.

r002.rationale: It advocates enforcing laws already in place instead of treating every AI harm as requiring a new legal framework.
